#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Unit test for the empty JSON response fix.
This test can be integrated into the main test suite.
"""

import pytest
import responses
from simple_rest_client.api import API


@responses.activate
def test_empty_json_response_handling():
    """Test that empty JSON responses are handled gracefully without JSONDecodeError."""
    # Create API instance
    api = API(
        api_root_url='https://api.example.com',
        timeout=10
    )
    api.add_resource(resource_name='users')

    # Mock a 204 No Content response with empty body but JSON content-type
    responses.add(
        responses.DELETE,
        'https://api.example.com/users/1',
        body='',  # Empty body (typical for 204 responses)
        status=204,
        content_type='application/json'
    )

    # This should not raise JSONDecodeError
    response = api.users.destroy(1)
    
    # Assertions
    assert response.status_code == 204
    assert response.body == {}  # Should return empty dict for empty JSON
    assert response.method == 'DELETE'


@responses.activate
def test_whitespace_only_json_response_handling():
    """Test that whitespace-only JSON responses are handled gracefully."""
    # Create API instance
    api = API(
        api_root_url='https://api.example.com',
        timeout=10
    )
    api.add_resource(resource_name='users')

    # Mock a response with only whitespace but JSON content-type
    responses.add(
        responses.DELETE,
        'https://api.example.com/users/1',
        body='   \n\t  ',  # Whitespace only
        status=204,
        content_type='application/json'
    )

    # This should not raise JSONDecodeError
    response = api.users.destroy(1)
    
    # Assertions
    assert response.status_code == 204
    assert response.body == {}  # Should return empty dict for whitespace-only JSON
    assert response.method == 'DELETE'


@responses.activate
def test_normal_json_response_still_works():
    """Test that normal JSON responses still work correctly."""
    # Create API instance
    api = API(
        api_root_url='https://api.example.com',
        timeout=10
    )
    api.add_resource(resource_name='users')

    # Mock a normal JSON response
    responses.add(
        responses.GET,
        'https://api.example.com/users/1',
        json={'id': 1, 'name': 'John Doe'},
        status=200,
        content_type='application/json'
    )

    # This should work as before
    response = api.users.retrieve(1)
    
    # Assertions
    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert response.body == {'id': 1, 'name': 'John Doe'}
    assert response.method == 'GET'


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Run the tests
    test_empty_json_response_handling()
    test_whitespace_only_json_response_handling()
    test_normal_json_response_still_works()
    print("All tests passed!")

#!/usr/bin/env python
"""Test to validate that the subject_info fix works correctly."""

import tempfile
import numpy as np
import mne
from mne_bids import write_raw_bids, read_raw_bids, BIDSPath
from mne_bids.read import _handle_participants_reading


def test_subject_info_valid_keys_only():
    """Test that only valid MNE subject_info keys are added."""
    
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:
        # Create participants.tsv with valid and invalid columns
        participants_file = f'{tmpdir}/participants.tsv'
        with open(participants_file, 'w') as f:
            f.write('participant_id\tsex\thand\theight\tweight\tage\tcustom_field\tfirst_name\tlast_name\n')
            f.write('sub-01\tF\tR\t180.5\t70.5\t25\tcustom_value\tJohn\tSmith\n')
            
        # Create a raw object
        raw = mne.io.RawArray(np.random.randn(1, 1000), 
                             mne.create_info(ch_names=['test'], sfreq=100))
        raw.info['subject_info'] = {}
        
        # Test the function directly
        result_raw = _handle_participants_reading(participants_file, raw, 'sub-01')
        
        # Check subject_info contents
        subject_info = result_raw.info['subject_info']
        print("Subject info contents:")
        for key, value in subject_info.items():
            print(f"  {key}: {value}")
        
        # Valid MNE subject_info keys
        valid_keys = {'id', 'his_id', 'last_name', 'first_name', 'middle_name', 
                     'birthday', 'sex', 'hand'}
        
        # Check that only valid keys are present
        actual_keys = set(subject_info.keys())
        invalid_keys = actual_keys - valid_keys
        
        assert len(invalid_keys) == 0, f"Found invalid keys in subject_info: {invalid_keys}"
        
        # Check that expected valid keys are present
        assert 'his_id' in subject_info
        assert 'sex' in subject_info  
        assert 'hand' in subject_info
        assert 'first_name' in subject_info
        assert 'last_name' in subject_info
        assert subject_info['his_id'] == 'sub-01'
        assert subject_info['sex'] == 2  # Female -> 2
        assert subject_info['hand'] == 1  # Right -> 1
        assert subject_info['first_name'] == 'John'
        assert subject_info['last_name'] == 'Smith'
        
        # Check that invalid keys are NOT present
        assert 'height' not in subject_info
        assert 'weight' not in subject_info
        assert 'age' not in subject_info
        assert 'custom_field' not in subject_info
        assert 'participant_id' not in subject_info  # Should be converted to his_id
        
        print("✅ All assertions passed!")

   119	
   120	There are 2 different APIs you can use with this library.
   121	
   122	* `smbprotocol`: Low level interface that can do whatever you want but quite verbose
   123	* `smbclient`: Higher level interface that implements the builtin `os` and `os.path` file system functions but for SMB support

   125	The `examples` folder contains some examples of both the high and low level
   126	interface but for everyday user's it is recommended to use `smbclient` as it

   128	
   129	### smbclient Interface
   130	
   131	The higher level interface `smbclient` is designed to make this library easier
   132	for people to use for simple and common use cases. It is designed to replicate
   133	the builtin `os` and `os.path` filesystem functions like `os.open()`,
   134	`os.stat()`, and `os.path.exists()`. It is also designed to handle connections
   135	to a DFS target unlike `smbprotocol`.
   136	
   137	A connection made by `smbclient` is kept in a pool and re-used for future
   138	requests to the same server until the Python process exists. This makes
   139	authentication simple and only required for the first call to the server. Any
   140	DFS referrals are also cached in that Python process. This optimises any
   141	future requests to that same DFS namespace.
   142	
   143	The functions in `smbclient` have a global config object that can be used to
   144	set any connection defaults to use for any future connections. It can also be
   145	used to specify any domain based DFS settings for more advanced setups. It is
   146	recommended to use `ClientConfig()` to set any global credentials like so:
   147	
   148	```python
   149	import smbclient
   150	
   151	smbclient.ClientConfig(username='user', password='password')
   152	```
   153	
   154	The `ClientConfig` is a singleton and any future instanciations of that
   155	object will just update the keys being set. You can set the following keys on
   156	the `ClientConfig`:
   157	
   158	* `client_guid`: The client GUID to identify the client to the server on a new connection
   159	* `username`: The default username to use when creating a new SMB session if explicit credentials weren't set
   160	* `password`: The default password to use for authentication
   161	* `domain_controller`: The domain controller hostname. This is useful for environments with DFS servers as it is used to identify the DFS domain information automatically
   162	* `skip_dfs`: Whether to skip doing any DFS resolution, useful if there is a bug or you don't want to waste any roundtrip requesting referrals
   163	* `auth_protocol`: The authentication protocol to use; `negotiate` (default), `kerberos`, or `ntlm`
   164	* `require_secure_negotiate`: Control whether the client validates the negotiation info when connecting to a share (default: `True`).
   165	    * More information can be found on [SMB3 Secure Dialect Negotiation](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/blogs/openspecification/smb3-secure-dialect-negotiation)
   166	
   167	As well as setting the default credentials on the `ClientConfig` you can also
   168	specify the credentials and other connection parameters on each `smbclient`
   169	function or when registering a new server. These functions accept the
   170	following kwargs:
   171	
   172	* `username`: The username used to connect to the share
   173	* `password`: The password used to connect to the share
   174	* `port`: Override the default port (`445`) to connect to
   175	* `encrypt`: Whether to force encryption on the connection, requires SMBv3 or newer on the remote server (default: `False`)
   176	* `connection_timeout`: Override the connection timeout in seconds (default: `60`)
   177

   180	having to be explicitly set. If no ticket has been retrieved or you wish to use
   181	different credentials then set the default credentials on the `ClientConfig`
   182	or specify `username` and `password` on the first request to the server.

   188	import smbclient
   189	
   190	# Optional - specify the default credentials to use on the global config object
   191	smbclient.ClientConfig(username='user', password='pass')
   192	
   193	# Optional - register the credentials with a server (overrides ClientConfig for that server)

def close(self):
        with self._sock_lock:
            if self.connected:
                log.info("Disconnecting DirectTcp socket")

                # Sending shutdown first will tell the recv thread (for both select and recv) that the socket has data
                # which returns b'' meaning it was closed.
                try:
                    self._sock.shutdown(socket.SHUT_RDWR)
                except OSError as e:  # pragma: no cover
                    # Avoid collecting coverage here to avoid CI failing due to race condition differences
                    if e.errno != errno.ENOTCONN:
                        raise

                # This is even more special, we cannot close the socket if we are in the middle of a select or recv().
                # Doing so causes either a timeout (bad!) or bad fd descriptor (somewhat bad). By shutting down the
                # socket first then waiting until recv() has exited the critical select/recv section we can ensure we
                # gracefully handle client side socket closures both here and our recv thread without any extra waits
                # or exceptions.
                with self._close_lock:
                    self._sock.close()
                    self.connected = False

#!/usr/bin/env python3

"""
Final verification test for the thread cleanup fix.
This test verifies that the msg_worker thread is properly joined during disconnect.
"""

import threading
import time
import uuid
from unittest.mock import patch, MagicMock
from smbprotocol.connection import Connection


def count_active_msg_worker_threads():
    """Count currently active msg_worker threads."""
    count = 0
    active_threads = []
    for thread in threading.enumerate():
        if thread.name.startswith('msg_worker-') and thread.is_alive():
            count += 1
            active_threads.append(thread.name)
    return count, active_threads


def test_thread_cleanup_after_disconnect():
    """Test that msg_worker threads are properly cleaned up after disconnect."""
    print("=== Final Verification Test ===")
    
    initial_thread_count, initial_threads = count_active_msg_worker_threads()
    print(f"Initial active msg_worker threads: {initial_thread_count}")
    if initial_threads:
        print(f"  Threads: {initial_threads}")
    
    # Create connection
    connection = Connection(uuid.uuid4(), "test-server", 445)
    print(f"Created connection: {connection.server_name}:{connection.port}")
    
    # Verify _t_worker attribute exists and is initialized to None
    assert hasattr(connection, '_t_worker'), "Connection should have _t_worker attribute"
    assert connection._t_worker is None, "_t_worker should be None initially"
    print("✅ _t_worker attribute properly initialized")
    
    # Mock the transport and negotiation to avoid actual network calls
    # but still allow thread creation
    with patch('smbprotocol.connection.Tcp') as mock_tcp:
        mock_transport = MagicMock()
        mock_transport.connected = True
        mock_tcp.return_value = mock_transport
        
        # Mock the negotiation to succeed quickly
        with patch.object(connection, '_send_smb2_negotiate') as mock_negotiate:
            mock_response = MagicMock()
            # Set up the mock response with required values
            mock_response.__getitem__.return_value.get_value.side_effect = [
                0x0300,  # dialect_revision (SMB_3_0_0)
                1024 * 1024,  # max_transact_size
                1024 * 1024,  # max_read_size
                1024 * 1024,  # max_write_size
                uuid.uuid4(),  # server_guid
                b'',  # buffer/gss_negotiate_token
            ]
            mock_response.__getitem__.return_value.has_flag.return_value = False
            mock_negotiate.return_value = mock_response
            
            # Patch the _process_message_thread to not run indefinitely
            original_process_thread = connection._process_message_thread
            def mock_process_thread():
                # Simple mock that just sleeps briefly then exits
                time.sleep(0.01)
                
            with patch.object(connection, '_process_message_thread', side_effect=mock_process_thread):
                print("Calling connect()...")
                connection.connect()
                
                # Small delay to let thread start
                time.sleep(0.01)
                
                # Check that _t_worker is now set
                assert connection._t_worker is not None, "_t_worker should be set after connect"
                assert isinstance(connection._t_worker, threading.Thread), "_t_worker should be a Thread"
                print(f"✅ Thread created: {connection._t_worker.name}")
                
                # Check thread count
                mid_thread_count, mid_threads = count_active_msg_worker_threads()
                print(f"Active msg_worker threads after connect: {mid_thread_count}")
                if mid_threads:
                    print(f"  Threads: {mid_threads}")
    
    # Now test disconnect
    print("Calling disconnect()...")
    connection.disconnect()
    
    # Check that thread was joined (should be dead)
    if connection._t_worker is not None:
        if not connection._t_worker.is_alive():
            print("✅ Thread properly joined and finished")
        else:
            print("⚠️  Thread still alive after disconnect (may be OK due to timeout)")
    
    # Wait a moment and check final thread count
    time.sleep(0.05)
    final_thread_count, final_threads = count_active_msg_worker_threads()
    print(f"Final active msg_worker threads: {final_thread_count}")
    if final_threads:
        print(f"  Threads: {final_threads}")
    
    # Should have same or fewer threads than we started with
    if final_thread_count <= initial_thread_count:
        print("✅ No stray msg_worker threads detected")
        return True
    else:
        print("❌ Stray msg_worker threads detected")
        return False


def test_edge_cases():
    """Test edge cases for the thread handling."""
    print("\n=== Edge Case Tests ===")
    
    # Test disconnect without connect (should not crash)
    connection = Connection(uuid.uuid4(), "test-server", 445)
    assert connection._t_worker is None
    
    print("Testing disconnect without connect...")
    try:
        connection.disconnect()
        print("✅ Disconnect without connect handled gracefully")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"❌ Error during disconnect without connect: {e}")
        return False
    
    # Test multiple disconnect calls
    print("Testing multiple disconnect calls...")

        connection.disconnect()
        connection.disconnect()
        print("✅ Multiple disconnect calls handled gracefully")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"❌ Error during multiple disconnect calls: {e}")
        return False
    
    return True


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Final Verification of Thread Cleanup Fix")
    print("=" * 50)

   178	Command line usage
   179	------------------
   180	
   181	When installed, you can invoke faker from the command-line:
   182	
   183	.. code:: bash
   184	
   185	    faker [-h] [--version] [-o output]
   186	          [-l {bg_BG,cs_CZ,...,zh_CN,zh_TW}]
   187	          [-r REPEAT] [-s SEP]
   188	          [-i {package.containing.custom_provider otherpkg.containing.custom_provider}]
   189	          [fake] [fake argument [fake argument ...]]
   190	
   191	Where:
   192	
   193	-  ``faker``: is the script when installed in your environment, in
   194	   development you could use ``python -m faker`` instead
   195	
   196	-  ``-h``, ``--help``: shows a help message
   197	
   198	-  ``--version``: shows the program's version number
   199	
   200	-  ``-o FILENAME``: redirects the output to the specified filename
   201	
   202	-  ``-l {bg_BG,cs_CZ,...,zh_CN,zh_TW}``: allows use of a localized
   203	   provider
   204	
   205	-  ``-r REPEAT``: will generate a specified number of outputs
   206	
   207	-  ``-s SEP``: will generate the specified separator after each
   208	   generated output
   209	
   210	-  ``-i {my.custom_provider other.custom_provider}`` list of additional custom providers to use.
   211	   Note that is the import path of the package containing your Provider class, not the custom Provider class itself.
   212	
   213	-  ``fake``: is the name of the fake to generate an output for, such as
   214	   ``name``, ``address``, or ``text``
   215	
   216	-  ``[fake argument ...]``: optional arguments to pass to the fake (e.g. the profile fake takes an optional list of comma separated field names as the first argument)
   217	
   218	Examples:
   219	
   220	.. code:: bash
   221	
   222	    $ faker address
   223	    968 Bahringer Garden Apt. 722
   224	    Kristinaland, NJ 09890
   225	
   226	    $ faker -l de_DE address
   227	    Samira-Niemeier-Allee 56
   228	    94812 Biedenkopf
   229	
   230	    $ faker profile ssn,birthdate
   231	    {'ssn': u'628-10-1085', 'birthdate': '2008-03-29'}
   232	
   233	    $ faker -r=3 -s=";" name
   234	    Willam Kertzmann;
   235	    Josiah Maggio;
   236	    Gayla Schmitt;
   237	
   238	How to create a Provider
   239	------------------------
   240	
   241	.. code:: python
   242	
   243	    from faker import Faker
   244	    fake = Faker()
   245	
   246	    # first, import a similar Provider or use the default one
   247	    from faker.providers import BaseProvider
   248	
   249	    # create new provider class. Note that the class name _must_ be ``Provider``.
   250	    class Provider(BaseProvider):
   251	        def foo(self):
   252	            return 'bar'
   253	
   254	    # then add new provider to faker instance
   255	    fake.add_provider(Provider)
   256	
   257	    # now you can use:
   258	    fake.foo()
   259	    > 'bar'
   260	
   261	How to customize the Lorem Provider
   262	-----------------------------------
   263	
   264	You can provide your own sets of words if you don't want to use the
   265	default lorem ipsum one. The following example shows how to do it with a list of words picked from `cakeipsum <http://www.cupcakeipsum.com/>`__ :
   266	
   267	.. code:: python
   268	
   269	    from faker import Faker
   270	    fake = Faker()
   271	
   272	    my_word_list = [
   273	    'danish','cheesecake','sugar',
   274	    'Lollipop','wafer','Gummies',
   275	    'sesame','Jelly','beans',
   276	    'pie','bar','Ice','oat' ]
   277	
   278	    fake.sentence()
   279	    #'Expedita at beatae voluptatibus nulla omnis.'
   280	
   281	    fake.sentence(ext_word_list=my_word_list)
   282	    # 'Oat beans oat Lollipop bar cheesecake.'
   283	
   284	
   285	How to use with Factory Boy
   286	---------------------------
   287	
   288	`Factory Boy` already ships with integration with ``Faker``. Simply use the
   289	``factory.Faker`` method of ``factory_boy``:
   290	
   291	.. code:: python
   292	
   293	    import factory
   294	    from myapp.models import Book
   295	
   296	    class BookFactory(factory.Factory):
   297	        class Meta:
   298	            model = Book
   299	
   300	        title = factory.Faker('sentence', nb_words=4)
   301	        author_name = factory.Faker('name')
   302	
   303	Accessing the `random` instance
   304	-------------------------------
   305	
   306	The ``.random`` property on the generator returns the instance of ``random.Random``
   307	used to generate the values:
   308	
   309	.. code:: python
   310	
   311	    from faker import Faker
   312	    fake = Faker()
   313	    fake.random
   314	    fake.random.getstate()
   315	
   316	By default all generators share the same instance of ``random.Random``, which
   317	can be accessed with ``from faker.generator import random``. Using this may
   318	be useful for plugins that want to affect all faker instances.
   319	
   320	Seeding the Generator
   321	---------------------
   322	
   323	When using Faker for unit testing, you will often want to generate the same
   324	data set. For convenience, the generator also provide a ``seed()`` method, which
   325	seeds the shared random number generator. Calling the same methods with the
   326	same version of faker and seed produces the same results.
   327	
   328	.. code:: python
   329	
   330	    from faker import Faker
   331	    fake = Faker()
   332	    fake.seed(4321)
   333	
   334	    print(fake.name())
   335	    > Margaret Boehm
   336	
   337	Each generator can also be switched to its own instance of ``random.Random``,
   338	separate to the shared one, by using the ``seed_instance()`` method, which acts
   339	the same way. For example:
   340	
   341	.. code-block:: python
   342	
   343	    from faker import Faker
   344	    fake = Faker()
   345	    fake.seed_instance(4321)
   346	
   347	    print(fake.name())
   348	    > Margaret Boehm
   349	
   350	Please note that as we keep updating datasets, results are not guaranteed to be
   351	consistent across patch versions. If you hardcode results in your test, make sure
   352	you pinned the version of ``Faker`` down to the patch number.
